front.title: Signed Attestation Rows of the CIRIS Epistemic Grammar and Their Relationship to SCITT
front.workgroup: Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust

abstract.t: The CIRIS Epistemic Grammar (CEG) records claims between parties as signed rows. Each row is one JSON object, canonicalised with the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) and signed twice: once with Ed25519 and once with ML-DSA-65, where the ML-DSA-65 signature covers the canonical bytes followed by the Ed25519 signature. Every row has one of five types: a claim, a delegation, a replacement, a withdrawal, or a recantation. A node admits a row only after a fixed set of checks, and it refuses a failing row with a named reason.

This document specifies the signed object, the signing input, the signature construction, and the admission checks, so that a second implementation can produce and verify the same bytes. It then describes how these rows relate to the roles of the SCITT architecture (RFC 9943), and where they differ from a SCITT Transparency Service. It defines no new SCITT mechanism and requests no IANA action.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: CEG is the row format of the CIRIS system, in which people, devices, communities and AI agents make claims about each other and act on them. It is defined normatively in the CIRIS Constitution . This document restates the parts of that definition that another implementation needs in order to interoperate at the byte level.
Three goals shape the format:

list.t: Any party holding a row can recompute its signing bytes exactly. Signatures are over a canonical form, and every point where JSON or JCS would let one encoding produce two byte strings is fixed. Two encodings of one meaning can still exist (an explicit default, or a one-element scope written as a string); they are different rows with different bytes, and both verify ().
Rows exchanged between nodes have to resist forgery by an attacker with a quantum computer. Every such row carries an ML-DSA-65 signature beside the Ed25519 signature , and both MUST verify.
The set of row types is closed, so that every row is subject to the same admission rules. New kinds of claim are new values of dimension, never new types.

section.t: SCITT defines an architecture for registering signed statements with a Transparency Service and returning receipts that prove registration. CEG rows play a similar role in their own system, but the two were designed separately and differ in encoding and in how proofs are delivered. describes the relationship. A COSE encoding of CEG rows is out of scope; says what one would need to cover.

section.name: Scope
section.t: In scope:

list.t: the signed object of an attestation row and its member set ();
the five row types ();
the canonical signing input ();
the hybrid signature and cosignatures ();
the admission checks, written as a SCITT Registration Policy ().

section.t: Informative only:

list.t: the safety properties the rows carry ();
the relationship to SCITT roles ();
the lifecycle of an agent's decision record ().

section.t: Out of scope: the transport between nodes, the storage schema, the meaning of individual claim families (the "dimension" namespace), and the governance rules that decide who may hold which role. defines each of these.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the terms Issuer, Signed Statement, Transparency Service, Registration Policy, Receipt, Transparent Statement, and Relying Party as defined in . It also uses:

dd.t: One signed attestation. On the wire it is a JSON object that carries the signed object and members beside it.
The JSON object named attestation_envelope inside a row. Its JCS image is the signing input. Nothing else in the row is signed.
The key that signs a row's signed object. It plays the SCITT Issuer role.
A party a row is about. attested_key_id names the primary subject; subject_key_ids lists any others, including parties that have no key.
A Producer emits rows. A Consumer verifies and reads rows. A Substrate stores and relays rows and applies the admission checks. One node is usually all three.

A fixed, case-sensitive ASCII string that names why a row was refused, so that two implementations agree on a refusal as well as on an acceptance. The tokens of are either all lowercase or all uppercase, and are compared byte for byte. A refusal of the shape of a row uses the token federation_malformed_row together with a reason from a closed set; "refused with reason R" in this document means that token with reason R.

A row at the local tier stays on the node that wrote it and is not replicated. A row at the federation tier may leave the node. Promotion from the local tier to the federation tier adds the ML-DSA-65 signature and does not change the signing input, so a promoted row is byte-identical to one written at the federation tier.

A key identifier of the form <label>-<fingerprint>, where the fingerprint is the first ten characters of the lowercase base32 encoding of the SHA-256 digest of the raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key. The label is chosen by the key holder.

section.name: Members of a Row
section.t: A row is a JSON object with the following members. Each is listed with its placement: signed members are inside the signing input; beside members travel with the row and are bound to it by a check, but are not signed.

texttable.title: Members of a row
texttable.c: key_id the row is primarily about.
Column copy of the signed instant.
Lowercase hex SHA-256 of the signing input.
key_id that produced the row's signature.

section.t: The seven members marked "mirrored" are repeated inside the signed object under the member row (). asserted_at and expires_at beside the row are read out of the signed object: a Substrate MUST refuse a row whose asserted_at column differs from the signed member, with reason typed_diverges_from_envelope, and expires_at is present beside the row exactly when it is present in the signed object. scrub_timestamp uses the instant form of . A Substrate MAY add members of its own beside the row; they are not part of this specification.

section.name: The Mirror
section.t: The signed object MUST contain a member row whose value is an object with exactly these members: attestation_id, attesting_key_id, attestation_type, attested_key_id, subject_key_ids, cohort_scope, and optionally weight. The set is closed. A Substrate MUST refuse a row:

list.t: whose signed object has no row member, with reason envelope_member_missing;
whose row object has any member not in this list, with reason envelope_row_member_unknown;
where any column beside the row differs from its mirror, with reason typed_diverges_from_envelope.

section.t: The mirror exists because the columns beside a row are what a Substrate indexes and a Consumer filters on. If those columns were not signed, a relay could change who a row is about or who may see it while the signature still verified.

subject_key_ids is always present in the mirror; an empty array means the row has no subject beyond attested_key_id. cohort_scope takes one of the values self, family, community, affiliations, species, biosphere, federation.

section.name: Members of the Signed Object
section.t: Besides row, every signed object carries:

dd.t: REQUIRED. The instant the attester makes the claim, in the form of .
REQUIRED. A string naming the claim family, for example expertise:cardiology:en:v1. Its grammar and registry are defined in and are not needed to verify a signature.
OPTIONAL. The instant after which the claim no longer stands.

section.t: Each row type adds members (). Claim families add members of their own. gives the full member list with types. A Consumer MUST preserve members it does not recognise when it relays a row, because removing one would change the signing input.

section.name: The Five Row Types
section.t: The attestation_type member takes exactly one of five values. A Substrate MUST refuse any other value, compared byte for byte, with attestation_type_unregistered. It MUST apply this check to rows it emits and to rows it receives.

dd.t: A claim about the attested key on the named dimension. It carries score and confidence, both numbers. Every positive or negative claim about a party is a scores row.

The attester authorises the attested key to sign on its behalf within scope, a set of strings, from delegation_valid_from until delegation_valid_until. For the scopes that lists as requiring a term, among them licensing, moderation and takedown, delegation_valid_until is REQUIRED and MUST be no more than 365 days after delegation_valid_from; a Substrate refuses a row that breaks this with delegation_term_required.
The attester replaces one of its own earlier rows, named by references_attestation_id. It MAY list the changed members in differs_in.
The attester retracts an earlier row, named by references_attestation_id, without saying the row was false. says who may withdraw a row.
The attester says one of its own earlier rows was false when it was made. Only the original attester can recant a row.

section.t: A withdrawal and a recantation are different statements. A withdrawal says "I no longer assert this"; a recantation says "this was wrong". Consumers can weigh them differently, and the subject of a row has authority over the first but not the second ().
A new kind of record is expressed as a new dimension on one of the five types, never as a sixth type.

section.name: The Signing Input
section.t: The signing input of a row is the JCS image of its signed object, as UTF-8 bytes. No other member of the row contributes to it.

JCS fixes member order, whitespace, string escaping and number formatting, but leaves several choices open that would let two Producers encode the same claim differently. The rules in this section close them.

section.name: Absent, Never Null, Never Materialised
section.t: An optional member is unset by being absent. A Producer MUST NOT emit an optional member with the JSON value null. A Substrate MUST refuse a row whose signed object contains an optional member set to null, with federation_malformed_row and the reason envelope_member_null.

A default is applied when a row is read, never when it is encoded. A Producer that writes a member at its default value and a Producer that omits it produce different signing bytes; both rows verify, and both mean the same thing. A Substrate that stores or relays a row MUST NOT add a defaulted member or remove one, because either change alters the signing input.

section.name: Arrays
section.t: Each array member is declared as either a set or a sequence. The declarations are in .

list.t: A set MUST be sorted in ascending order of the JCS serialisation of each element, compared as sequences of UTF-16 code units (the comparison JCS uses for member names), and its elements MUST be unique. A Substrate MUST refuse a row with an unsorted or duplicated set, with federation_set_semantics_unsorted naming the member. It MUST NOT sort the set itself, because that would change the signing input.
A sequence keeps the order its author gave it.

section.t: subject_key_ids, scope and differs_in are sets. evidence_refs is a sequence. An array without a declaration is a set.
The scope member MAY be a single string or an array. A single string denotes the one-element set; a Substrate MUST NOT rewrite one form into the other.

section.name: Strings That Carry Bytes
section.t: JSON has no byte type. Hashes, digests and raw key material inside the signing input are lowercase hexadecimal, with no prefix and no separators. Members declared as base64 use the standard alphabet of with padding and no line breaks.

An element of subject_key_ids is either a key_id, copied byte for byte from the key's record, or a tagged canonical identifier of the form canonical:<hashalg>:<hex> for a party that has no key. The tag is part of the signed string. A Substrate MUST refuse an element whose tag is not in lowercase, and MUST NOT repair it.

section.name: Instants
section.t: Every instant inside the signing input is written as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ: UTC, the literal uppercase Z, and exactly three fractional digits. This is a profile of . A Producer MUST emit this form. A Substrate MUST refuse any other form inside the signing input with reason envelope_member_invalid, even though a signature over those bytes would still verify.

section.name: Numbers
section.t: JCS serialises numbers as IEEE 754 binary64 values. A Producer MUST convert every number to its finite binary64 value before computing the signing input, and MUST fail, rather than emit a row, for a number that has none (for example 1e1000). A parser that keeps numbers at arbitrary precision would otherwise emit bytes that another implementation cannot reproduce.

section.name: Size
section.t: The signing input MUST NOT exceed 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes). A Substrate MUST refuse a larger row on every path by which rows reach it, with ENVELOPE_TOO_LARGE. Because the limit is on canonical bytes, it can only be decided after parsing; each intake path therefore also needs a local limit on how many bytes it will read before it stops. That local limit MUST NOT be less than 1 MiB and is not part of the interoperable contract. A Substrate that receives a non-canonical serialisation larger than its local limit MAY refuse it even if its canonical form would fit; the interoperable serialisation is the canonical one. Larger content travels outside the row and is named in evidence_refs by its hash.

section.name: The Content Hash
section.t: original_content_hash is the lowercase hex SHA-256 digest of the signing input. A Substrate MUST recompute it when it receives a row and MUST refuse a row whose value differs.

section.name: The Hybrid Signature
section.t: The attester's signature has two parts, made with the attester's key pair:

list.t: scrub_signature_classical is the Ed25519 signature over the signing input.

scrub_signature_pqc is the ML-DSA-65 signature over the signing input followed by the 64 raw bytes of the Ed25519 signature, computed with ML-DSA.Sign and an empty context string. HashML-DSA is not used.

section.t: Both values are encoded in base64. scrub_key_id MUST equal attesting_key_id. A Consumer verifies each part against the public keys it holds for that key_id. At the federation tier both parts MUST verify; a row with only the Ed25519 part is not admitted there. There is no configuration that turns the ML-DSA-65 check off.

In the terms of this is a nested hybrid: the second signature covers the message and the first signature (; terminology from ). Because the ML-DSA-65 input contains the Ed25519 signature, an ML-DSA-65 signature taken from one row cannot be paired with a different Ed25519 signature. The construction is not the composite signature of and , in which both components sign the same prefixed message representative and neither covers the other. Deployed rows use the nested form, and this document describes what they carry.

A Producer MAY use either the hedged or the deterministic variant of ML-DSA.Sign. A Consumer MUST accept any valid signature and MUST NOT expect the ML-DSA-65 part to be byte-identical across signers. The reference implementation uses the deterministic variant, so the vectors in reproduce bit for bit from their seeds.

section.name: Cosignatures
section.t: A row MAY carry further signatures over the same signing input in additional_scrubs, an array of objects with these members:

dd.t: REQUIRED. The cosigner's key_id.
REQUIRED. Ed25519 over the signing input.
REQUIRED at the federation tier. ML-DSA-65 over the signing input followed by this entry's Ed25519 signature.
OPTIONAL. When the cosignature was applied.

section.t: Cosignatures are beside the signed object, not inside it, because a signature cannot be part of the bytes it signs. Adding a cosignature therefore changes neither the signing input nor the attester's signature. An entry carries no role: a Consumer decides what role a cosigner holds from its own record of the relevant group or roster, at the row's asserted_at.

A claim family can require a quorum. It does so by naming where the rule comes from (for example the group the row is about), and a Substrate admits the row only when the attester and the cosigners that verify and hold a seat in that group meet the group's rule. A cosignature that does not verify, or whose key holds no seat, is not counted; it is not an error.

section.name: Keys
section.t: A Consumer resolves a key_id to an Ed25519 public key and an ML-DSA-65 public key through its own key directory, which is populated by key records that are themselves signed (). defines how keys are registered and revoked. Verification also requires that:

list.t: the fingerprint in the key_id MUST match the SHA-256 digest of the Ed25519 public key the directory returns, so a directory entry cannot be substituted for another key with the same label; and
a revoked key MAY carry an instant revoked_after, so that rows the key signed before that instant still stand and rows signed after it do not.

section.name: The v62 Edition: CBOR and COSE
section.t: A later release candidate of the grammar, the one that accompanies the substrate's v62, moves the signed object from JSON with JCS to CBOR with COSE, without changing what a row says. A row becomes one COSE_Sign1, a SCITT Signed Statement as defines it: the row type and family in the content type, the signer's key identifier in kid, the issuer and subject in the CWT Claims header, which removes the mirror of ; a quorum () becomes one Signed Statement per signer over the same payload, found by a statement identifier that excludes the signatures; the canonical form is the deterministic encoding of as the CBOR working group's deterministic-encoding profile fixes it; the hybrid of becomes the composite ML-DSA-65 with Ed25519 construction of the JOSE and COSE working group, carried under a private-use algorithm identifier until one is assigned; keys are composite COSE keys identified by their thumbprints; receipts over the provenance and stream logs are COSE Receipts over the tree of RFC 9162. Every row signed under the object of this document verifies as itself under that edition. The relationship to SCITT described in is unchanged in one respect: there is still no Transparency Service in the grammar's own architecture, and the rows are statements any Transparency Service could register.

section.name: Admission as a Registration Policy
section.t: lets each Transparency Service define a Registration Policy: the checks a Signed Statement must pass before it is registered. The CEG admission checks are such a policy. A Substrate MUST apply them, in any order, to every row before storing or relaying it, and MUST refuse a failing row with the token given. It MUST NOT truncate, repair or re-encode a row in order to admit it.

texttable.title: Admission checks
texttable.c: Type is one of the five

section.t: "(R) r" means the token federation_malformed_row with reason r.
The namespace rules that decide whether a dimension resolves, and their tokens, are defined in and are outside the scope of this document.

section.name: Who May Withdraw a Row
section.t: A withdraws row against a target row T is admitted when its attester meets any one of these rules:

list.t: It is T's attester.
It appears in T's subject_key_ids.

It holds an unexpired delegates_to chain whose scope includes consent_revocation, from a canonical identifier that appears in T's subject_key_ids. This is how an agent holding data on behalf of a party with no key can act on that party's request.
It holds an unexpired delegates_to from a key that meets rule 1, 2 or 3.

section.t: Two further rules take precedence:

list.t: If T carries cosignatures, rules 1 to 4 do not apply. T is withdrawn only by a withdraws that is itself cosigned under T's quorum rule.

A subject cannot use rules 2 to 4 to withdraw a third party's adverse claim about itself, such as a detection or a licensing decision. lists the families this covers. The subject's route is to dispute the claim with a row of its own.

section.t: Recantation is not covered by these rules. Only T's attester can recant T.

section.name: The Safety Model the Rows Carry
section.t: This section is informative. is normative for every rule it summarises, and the section numbers given are those of .

CEG serves a network with no central operator. No party can enforce a safety rule for the others, so each rule has to be carried by the rows themselves and checked by each node on its own. This section says which member or check carries each property, and what is not claimed.

section.name: Two Planes
section.t: The network has a public plane and a private plane. The CIRIS documents call them the lightnet and the darknet.

The identity plane (lightnet) is public. Key records, announced transport destinations and trust roots are visible to every node, and the plane makes no anonymity claim. A node attributes every inbound message to a key before any handler sees it. A device that has not yet been bound to an owner can still open a connection, but only under its own self-signed key, so it is unowned but never anonymous (CC 3.2).

The group plane (darknet) is derived from the identity plane. Each member of a family or community computes the group's address from directory state it already holds (a per-group HKDF), so the address is never announced and an outsider cannot map an address to a group or fetch its content (CC 5.2, CC 5.4.6). An observer of link traffic can still see which node opens links to some derived address, and the timing and size of that traffic (CC 5.4.6). A node never announces that it holds content scoped to a family or community outside that group. Members relay for members.

section.name: Consent-Bounded Flow
section.t: The rows apply the idea of contextual integrity: information flows appropriately when the flow matches the norms of the context it came from. Each row signs its own context. attesting_key_id says who sent it, attested_key_id and subject_key_ids say whom it is about, and cohort_scope says who may see it. All of these are in the mirror (), so a relay cannot change them without breaking the signature.

A Consumer accepts a row only if it trusts the attester's root or has consented to receive from the attester, and a row reaches no one else (CC 4.4.3.8). A row defaults to the smallest scope that fits its purpose; federation scope, the public commons, is an explicit choice (CC 1.13.3.4). Consent is itself a row, and a subject can withdraw a row about itself (). Content in a private scope is never scanned. Known abuse images are checked for only when content is moved to federation scope or posted to a public room (CC 1.13.3.4).

section.name: Accountable Key Relationships
section.t: Some parties cannot accept obligations for themselves. The rows give each of them a named human:

list.t: A key whose identity type includes agent or node MUST have a steward: a human identity with a live delegates_to row binding the key. Without one, the key cannot be admitted to any family, community or organisation. It MAY trust and serve infrastructure communities without a steward (CC 3.2).
A minor has a guardian bound by a signed row (CC 3.4.13).
A community has a named moderator at all times. If the moderator lapses, the most trusted member is promoted in the same step (CC 4.5.4).

section.name: A Bounded Human Halt
section.t: A trust root names a small set of human holders. Any one holder can pause the agents that accepted that root with a single signed row. A pause by one holder lapses after 24 hours unless a majority of the holders confirms it, and a majority ends it. A pause stops agents from acting; it does not touch stored data, messages or network service. A root can tell a node to share less, never more. A node that never accepted the root is not affected, and any node can leave a root by withdrawing one row (CC 4.2.1, CC 4.2.6).

section.name: What Is Not Claimed
section.t: Where speaks of anonymity, it means anonymity toward outsiders: a group's existence, and what its members do in it, are hidden from non-members. Beyond that:

list.t: The identity plane is not anonymous.

No multi-hop anonymity is provided today, and the deployed design does not resist a global passive observer of traffic. An opt-in anonymous tier using onion routing is planned for deployments that need that protection (CC 1.13.3.1). It is not yet specified in or shipped, and this document does not describe it.
Members of a group can read, and keep, what the group shares. Ballots within a group are accountable to its members, not secret from them.
Nothing is detected inside private groups. The design declines client-side scanning.

section.name: Relationship to SCITT
section.t: This section is informative.

texttable.title: SCITT roles and their CEG counterparts
texttable.c: A row: its signed object and the hybrid signature.
A Substrate with its RFC 6962 logs .

dd.t: requires Signed Statements to be COSE_Sign1 messages with an Issuer and a subject in the protected header. CEG rows are JSON with a JCS signing input, so a CEG row is not a SCITT Signed Statement. A profile that carried CEG rows through a SCITT service would wrap the signing input, or its hash, in a COSE_Sign1. ML-DSA-65 now has a COSE algorithm identifier , but the nested pair of has none, so such a profile would either carry two COSE signatures or change the construction. No such profile is defined.

has the Transparency Service evaluate its policy over the COSE headers and requires the policy itself to be registered, so that Auditors can reproduce the decision. The CEG checks read the whole signed object, and they are fixed by rather than registered as statements. Any party can reproduce an admission decision from the row and the checks, but the checks are not themselves on the log.

A SCITT Receipt is a proof of inclusion, issued at registration and signed by the service, that the holder can present without the log. A CEG Substrate keeps RFC 6962 logs and returns inclusion and consistency proofs on request, against the current or a named tree size, but it does not issue a receipt when a row is admitted and does not store one with the row. The logs exist so that a node cannot show different histories to different peers, and so that any holder of the rows can recompute them. Issuing a COSE Receipt at admission, against a witness-cosigned tree head, would close this gap. It is not specified.

At the time of writing, the tree heads of deployed Substrates are signed by a single key. defines witness cosignature of tree heads and of trust-root lineages, but deployed roots have it turned off. A single signer can therefore equivocate between two forks until a peer compares heads.

SCITT leaves the meaning of a statement to its issuer. CEG fixes the five row types and requires every claim to name a registered dimension, so a Consumer can interpret any admitted row without out-of-band agreement.

section.name: Lifecycle of an Agent Decision
section.t: This section is informative.

Several individual SCITT drafts record AI agent actions as a sequence of statements: an authorisation before the act, a record of the act, and a refusal where the agent declined. In CEG the same events are rows. The reasoning steps before an act are rows in the decision families of . The act is recorded by one row whose dimension is trace:complete:v1, ending in a terminal result. A completed action, a refusal, and a deferral to a human are the same kind of row with different terminal results, so a Consumer reads all three the same way. Authority to act, and any transfer of it, is a delegates_to row.

section.t: Note to the RFC Editor: please remove this section before publication.

list.t: CIRISPersist does not yet refuse an unsorted or duplicated subject_key_ids set at admission, and does not yet emit the reasons content_hash_mismatch, envelope_row_member_unknown and subject_key_id_malformed, which named on 2026-10-21 ().
No COSE encoding of a row is defined ().
No second implementation exists ().

This section records the status of known implementations at the time of writing, as described in . Listing an implementation here does not imply endorsement.

dd.t: The storage and admission engine (Rust), CIRIS L3C, AGPL-3.0. Release v59.1.0 implements the signed object, the mirror checks, the hybrid signature and additional_scrubs. It does not yet refuse an unsorted or duplicated subject_key_ids set at admission. https://github.com/CIRISAI/CIRISPersist

Verification library (Rust), CIRIS L3C, AGPL-3.0. Provides the JCS implementation, the hybrid signer and verifier, and the RFC 6962 proofs. The test vectors in were produced with it. https://github.com/CIRISAI/CIRISVerify

section.t: No second, independent implementation of the full signing and admission path exists yet.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This section follows the guidance of .

dd.t: Every rule in closes a case in which a Producer and a Consumer that both follow JCS compute different bytes. The mismatch shows up only as a failed signature, with nothing to say which rule was broken. Implementations should test against the vectors in , and in particular against arrays, base64 variants and instants.

Only the signed object is signed. The mirror rule exists because the columns beside a row decide who a row is about and who may read it; an implementation that indexes those columns without checking them against the mirror lets a relay redirect a validly signed row.

A forger must produce both an Ed25519 signature over the signing input and an ML-DSA-65 signature over the signing input and that Ed25519 signature, but only against a verifier that checks both. notes that a verifier of a nested hybrid can be led to check only one part. A verifier that accepts Ed25519 alone gives no protection against an attacker able to forge Ed25519, and an attacker can always remove the ML-DSA-65 part of a row. For this reason the federation tier refuses a row without both parts and has no setting that relaxes the check. Rows below the federation tier MAY lack the ML-DSA-65 part and have only classical strength.

The key_id fingerprint is 50 bits. It is an identifier for lookup, not a commitment to a key. A verifier must use the full public key from its directory, and must check that the key's digest matches the fingerprint, as requires.

The withdrawal rules let parties other than the attester retract a row. The precedence rules in stop a subject from removing adverse findings about itself, and stop any single key from undoing a quorum's act.
Until witness cosignature is on, a Substrate's log head is signed by one key, and a Substrate can show different histories to different peers until the heads are compared ().
The 1 MiB limit applies after parsing. An implementation that reads an unbounded input in order to find out whether it fits is open to memory exhaustion; each intake path needs its own read limit.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: This section follows the guidance of .

dd.t: The label of a key_id is chosen by its holder and is sent in clear wherever the key_id appears. A label such as a person's device name reveals that name to every node that sees a row. For this reason a key revocation names the revoked key by the digest of its public key, not by its key_id.
A canonical identifier is a hash of a platform, entity kind and identifier. Where the identifier space is small, the hash can be reversed by enumeration.
cohort_scope limits which nodes may receive a row. It is signed, through the mirror, so a relay cannot widen it. It does not encrypt the row; a node inside the audience can read and keep it.
A withdraws row stops a claim from standing. It does not remove the original row from nodes that already hold it. defines a separate removal procedure.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

abstract.t: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. It was derived from the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard. JSON defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data.
This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON, repairs specification errors, and offers experience-based interoperability guidance.

front.title: JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)

abstract.t: Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

front.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)

abstract.t: The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation. These design goals make it different from earlier binary serializations such as ASN.1 and MessagePack.

This document obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial improvements, new details, and errata fixes while keeping full compatibility with the interchange format of RFC 7049. It does not create a new version of the format.

front.title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)

abstract.t: This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA). The algorithm is instantiated with recommended parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves. An example implementation and test vectors are provided.

front.title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings

abstract.t: This document describes the commonly used base 64, base 32, and base 16 encoding schemes. It also discusses the use of line-feeds in encoded data, use of padding in encoded data, use of non-alphabet characters in encoded data, use of different encoding alphabets, and canonical encodings. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

abstract.t: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for representation of dates and times using the Gregorian calendar.

front.title: Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDs)

abstract.t: This specification defines UUIDs (Universally Unique IDentifiers) -- also known as GUIDs (Globally Unique IDentifiers) -- and a Uniform Resource Name namespace for UUIDs. A UUID is 128 bits long and is intended to guarantee uniqueness across space and time. UUIDs were originally used in the Apollo Network Computing System (NCS), later in the Open Software Foundation's (OSF's) Distributed Computing Environment (DCE), and then in Microsoft Windows platforms.

This specification is derived from the OSF DCE specification with the kind permission of the OSF (now known as "The Open Group"). Information from earlier versions of the OSF DCE specification have been incorporated into this document. This document obsoletes RFC 4122.

front.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): A Notational Convention to Express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and JSON Data Structures

abstract.t: This document proposes a notational convention to express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures (RFC 7049). Its main goal is to provide an easy and unambiguous way to express structures for protocol messages and data formats that use CBOR or JSON.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While Verifiable Data Structures (VDSs) have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility and interoperability between different transparency services as well as compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

front.title: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard

author.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology

front.title: Certificate Transparency

abstract.t: This document describes an experimental protocol for publicly logging the existence of Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates as they are issued or observed, in a manner that allows anyone to audit certificate authority (CA) activity and notice the issuance of suspect certificates as well as to audit the certificate logs themselves. The intent is that eventually clients would refuse to honor certificates that do not appear in a log, effectively forcing CAs to add all issued certificates to the logs.
Logs are network services that implement the protocol operations for submissions and queries that are defined in this document.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: Guidelines for Writing RFC Text on Security Considerations

abstract.t: All RFCs are required to have a Security Considerations section. Historically, such sections have been relatively weak. This document provides guidelines to RFC authors on how to write a good Security Considerations section. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Privacy Considerations for Internet Protocols

abstract.t: This document offers guidance for developing privacy considerations for inclusion in protocol specifications. It aims to make designers, implementers, and users of Internet protocols aware of privacy-related design choices. It suggests that whether any individual RFC warrants a specific privacy considerations section will depend on the document's content.

front.title: Terminology for Post-Quantum Traditional Hybrid Schemes

abstract.t: One aspect of the transition to post-quantum algorithms in cryptographic protocols is the development of hybrid schemes that incorporate both post-quantum and traditional asymmetric algorithms. This document defines terminology for such schemes. It is intended to be used as a reference and, hopefully, to ensure consistency and clarity across different protocols, standards, and organisations.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts

abstract.t: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts prove properties of a Verifiable Data Structure (VDS) to a verifier. VDSs and associated Proof Types enable security properties, such as minimal disclosure, transparency, and non-equivocation. Transparency helps maintain trust over time and has been applied to certificates, end-to-end encrypted messaging systems, and supply chain security. This specification enables concise transparency-oriented systems by building on Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and COSE. The extensibility of the approach is demonstrated by providing CBOR encodings for Merkle inclusion and consistency proofs.

front.title: Hybrid Signature Spectrums

abstract.t: This document describes classification of design goals and security considerations for hybrid digital signature schemes, including proof composability, non-separability of the component signatures given a hybrid signature, backwards and forwards compatibility, hybrid generality, and Simultaneous Verification (SV).

front.title: ML-DSA for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE)

abstract.t: This document specifies JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) serializations for the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA), a Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) digital signature scheme defined in US NIST FIPS 204.

front.title: Composite Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) for use in X.509 Public Key Infrastructure

abstract.t: This document defines combinations of US NIST Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) in hybrid with traditional algorithms RSASSA-PKCS1-v1.5, RSASSA-PSS, ECDSA, Ed25519, and Ed448. These combinations are tailored to meet regulatory guidelines in certain regions. Composite ML-DSA is applicable in applications that use X.509 or PKIX data structures that accept ML-DSA, but where the operator wants extra protection against breaks or catastrophic bugs in ML-DSA, and where existential unforgeability (EUF-CMA) level security is acceptable.

front.title: PQ/T Hybrid Composite Signatures for JOSE and COSE

abstract.t: This document describes JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) serializations for Post- Quantum Traditional (PQ/T) hybrid composite signatures. The composite algorithms described combine the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) as the post-quantum component and either the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) or the Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) as the traditional component.
